claim: PAX8 is a prototype lineage-survival oncogene in epithelial ovarian cancer.
source: PAX8 is a prototype lineage-survival oncogene in epithelial ovarian cancer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to previous work (Cheung et al., 2011) and Project Achilles data mentioned in the introduction.

claim: PAX8 expression was potently inhibited by small-molecules against histone deacetylases (HDACs).
source: An image-based drug screen pinpointed that PAX8 expression was potently inhibited by small-molecules against histone deacetylases (HDACs).
evidence: This claim is supported by the high-throughput screen data presented in Figure 3 and related experimental results.

claim: HDAC blockade altered histone H3K27 acetylation occupancies and perturbed the super-enhancer topology associated with PAX8 gene locus.
source: Mechanistically, HDAC blockade altered histone H3K27 acetylation occupancies and perturbed the super-enhancer topology associated with PAX8 gene locus, resulting in epigenetic downregulation of PAX8 transcripts and related targets.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data showing H3K27ac changes at the PAX8 locus upon HDAC inhibitor treatment (Figure 4).

claim: HDAC antagonists efficaciously suppressed ovarian tumor growth and spreading as single agents.
source: HDAC antagonists efficaciously suppressed ovarian tumor growth and spreading as single agents, and exerted synergistic effects in combination with standard chemotherapy.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo xenograft experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: HDAC antagonists exerted synergistic effects in combination with standard chemotherapy.
source: HDAC antagonists efficaciously suppressed ovarian tumor growth and spreading as single agents, and exerted synergistic effects in combination with standard chemotherapy.
evidence: This is supported by combination treatment experiments in cell lines and PDX models shown in Figure 6.

claim: PAX8 belongs to an evolutionarily conserved family of nine nuclear transcription factors (PAX1-PAX9).
source: PAX8 belongs to an evolutionarily conserved family of nine nuclear transcription factors (PAX1-PAX9) that mostly play pivotal roles in lineage-dependent regulation during embryogenesis (Robson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Robson et al., 2006.

claim: PAX8 is restrictedly expressed in developing brain, thyroid, kidney, and Müllerian tract.
source: Mouse genetics studies reveal that PAX8 is restrictedly expressed in developing brain, thyroid, kidney, and Müllerian tract, from which the fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix and the upper third of the vagina originate.
evidence: This is based on mouse genetics studies cited in the text (Mansouri et al., 1998; Mittag et al., 2007).

claim: PAX8 knockout models are characterized by hypothyroidism and infertility.
source: As a result, PAX8 knockout models are characterized by hypothyroidism and infertility, due to severe dysgenesis of thyroid and reproductive duct, respectively (Mansouri et al., 1998; Mittag et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mouse knockout studies (Mansouri et al., 1998; Mittag et al., 2007).

claim: PAX8 is frequently upregulated and functionally essential in a major subset of ovarian cancer.
source: Specifically, PAX8 is frequently upregulated and functionally essential in a major subset of ovarian cancer, regardless of distinct somatic alterations or histologies (Cheung et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cheung et al., 2011 and Project Achilles data mentioned in the introduction.

claim: Modified cancer outlier profile analysis (COPA) on RNA sequencing data identified a lineage-specific PAX8 regulon in EOC.
source: In this study, we uncovered a lineage-specific PAX8 regulon in EOC by conducting modified cancer outlier profile analysis (COPA) (Tomlins et al., 2005) on RNA sequencing (RNAseq) data of a large cell line panel.
evidence: This is supported by the computational analysis described in the Results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The PAX8-FGF18 axis promotes ovarian tumor cell migration in an autocrine fashion.
source: The regulatory network was operative, as demonstrated by the PAX8-FGF18 axis in promoting ovarian tumor cell migration.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2 showing FGF18's role in cell migration.

claim: COPA identified eight lineage-restricted outliers (CDH6, CLDN16, FGF18, FOLR1, SLC34A2, SOX17, SPON1, WNT7A) in addition to PAX8.
source: In addition to PAX8, COPA complemented with pan-cancer analysis prioritized eight other lineage-restricted outliers (CDH6, CLDN16, FGF18, FOLR1, SLC34A2, SOX17, SPON1, WNT7A) displaying largely confined gene expression in ovarian cancer cell lines (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) and tumor specimens (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the COPA analysis and expression data shown in Figure 1D, 1E and supplements.

claim: The 9-gene outlier cluster was enriched in kidney, thyroid and fallopian tubes in normal tissues.
source: Intriguingly, a query of the normal tissue RNAseq data from Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project (GTEx Consortium, 2013) indicated that similar to PAX8 itself, the 9-gene outlier cluster was enriched in kidney, thyroid and fallopian tubes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of GTEx data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: PAX8 resides at the center of the outlier network, transcriptionally activating all other genes but FOLR1.
source: These investigations collectively supported that PAX8 resided at the very center of outlier network, transcriptionally activating all other genes but FOLR1, and thus acting as master regulator of a PAX8-centric regulon (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR-Cas9 knockout experiments and gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1F and supplements.

claim: PAX8 was ubiquitously expressed in various histopathological subtypes of ovarian carcinomas but not in adjacent or normal tissues.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Laury et al., 2011), immunohistochemical assessment of an EOC tissue microarray (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) containing 674 samples (Supplementary file 2) showed that PAX8 was ubiquitously expressed in various histopathological subtypes spanning serous, clear cell, endometrioid and mucinous ovarian carcinomas, but not within the adjacent or normal tissues (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical staining data from tissue microarrays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PAX8 knockdown resulted in downregulation of cell cycle and tumor metastasis related gene sets.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) pinpointed the anticipated suppressed pathways related to cell cycle upon PAX8 knockdown, and of interest, multiple significantly altered signaling modules promoting tumor metastasis (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by microarray and GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: PAX8 deficiency resulted in impaired cell proliferation and defective transwell migration.
source: In agreement with the microarray data, PAX8 deficiency resulted in not only impaired cell proliferation (Figure 2D) but also defective transwell migration (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CRISPR-Cas9 knockout experiments shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: PAX8 directly binds to the FGF18 promoter.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation coupled to detection by quantitative real-time PCR (ChIP-qPCR) proved that PAX8 directly bound to the FGF18 promoter (Figure 2H) and drove FGF18/FGFR gene expression (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: PAX8 drives FGF18/FGFR gene expression.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation coupled to detection by quantitative real-time PCR (ChIP-qPCR) proved that PAX8 directly bound to the FGF18 promoter (Figure 2H) and drove FGF18/FGFR gene expression (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data showing FGF18/FGFR expression changes upon PAX8 knockdown (Figure 2I).

claim: Exogenous FGF18 protein partly rescued cell migration defects caused by PAX8 depletion.
source: Backing up this hypothesis, exogenous supplement of FGF18 protein partly rescued the cell migration defects caused by sgRNA-mediated PAX8 depletion (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Panobinostat administration reduced PAX8 protein at dose- and time-dependent manners.
source: Western blotting ensured that panobinostat administration reduced PAX8 protein at dose- and time-dependent manners in KURAMOCHI (Figure 3E) and HEY (Figure 3F) cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Class I HDAC inhibitors (romidepsin and entinostat), but not class II HDAC inhibitors (tubacin and TMP195), specifically eliminated PAX8 accumulation.
source: Since three classical HDAC (HDAC1-11) classes existed and panobinostat was a pan-HDAC inhibitor, we further discovered that class I (romidepsin and entinostat), but not class II (tubacin and TMP195), HDAC blockade specifically eliminated PAX8 accumulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data comparing different HDAC inhibitor classes shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PAX8 was downregulated upon simultaneous knockout of three key class I HDAC members (HDAC1-3).
source: Corroboratively, PAX8 was downregulated upon simultaneous knockout of three key class I HDAC members (HDAC1-3) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), which led to impaired cell viability and motility (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CRISPR-Cas9 knockout experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: PAX8 overexpression partially reversed the antagonistic effects of HDAC inhibitors.
source: Importantly, PAX8 overexpression via lentiviral transduction (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) partially reversed the antagonistic effects of HDAC inhibitors (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments with PAX8 overexpression shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: H3K27ac occupancy profiles unveiled a typical super-enhancer structure around PAX8 promoter.
source: Strikingly, H3K27ac occupancy profiles unveiled a typical super-enhancer structure around PAX8 promoter, which displayed exceptionally intensive signal compared to its gene body (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HDAC inhibitors perturbed the enhancer topology by altering H3K27ac distribution ratios within PAX8 promoter zone relative to intron regions.
source: HDAC inhibitors probably perturbed the enhancer topology, as suggested by aberrantly altered H3K27ac distribution ratios within PAX8 promoter zone relative to the intron regions (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data showing changes in H3K27ac enrichment upon HDAC inhibitor treatment (Figure 4B).

claim: Panobinostat or romidepsin treatment resulted in rapid and pronounced downregulation of PAX8 transcripts.
source: In accordance with previous implications of super-enhancers in governing cell-type-specific genes (Whyte et al., 2013), panobinostat or romidepsin treatment resulted in rapid and pronounced downregulation of PAX8 transcripts (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: PAX8 was one of the hypersensitive genes to HDAC inhibitors at the transcriptome-wide scale.
source: At the transcriptome-wide scale, a time-course RNAseq assay in KURAMOCHI cells revealed that PAX8 was one of the hypersensitive genes to HDAC inhibitors, but not actinomycin D (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-course RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The PAX8 signature was preferentially enriched in HDAC-modulated transcripts.
source: We defined a PAX8 signature by merging uniformly deregulated targets upon PAX8 inactivation (Supplementary file 4), and subsequently showed that this gene set was preferentially enriched in HDAC-modulated transcripts (Figure 4G), reinforcing the link between HDAC and PAX8.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: NKX2-1 levels were notably reduced with HDAC blockage in lung adenocarcinoma models.
source: Gratifyingly, quantitative PCR indeed uncovered a notable reduction of NKX2-1 or SOX2 levels along with HDAC blockage in all tested lung adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma models, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data in lung cancer cell lines shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: SOX2 levels were notably reduced with HDAC blockage in squamous cell carcinoma models.
source: Gratifyingly, quantitative PCR indeed uncovered a notable reduction of NKX2-1 or SOX2 levels along with HDAC blockage in all tested lung adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma models, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data in squamous cell carcinoma lines shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Tumor development in mice was significantly hampered upon PAX8 knockout.
source: Reminiscent of our in vitro findings, tumor development in mice was significantly hampered upon PAX8 knockout compared with the control group (Figure 5A), as measured by the bioluminescence imaging.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo xenograft experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: PAX8 knockout resulted in evidently impaired abdominopelvic spreading in xenograft models.
source: Moreover, three-dimensional reconstruction of neoplastic lesions illustrated evidently impaired abdominopelvic spreading (Figure 5B), thus confirming the pro-migratory activity of PAX8.
evidence: This is demonstrated by 3D reconstruction of tumor lesions shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both tumor burden and metastatic dissemination were markedly reduced by panobinostat or romidepsin in HEY xenografts.
source: Similarly, when the HEY xenografts were treated with panobinostat or romidepsin, both tumor burden (Figure 5C) and metastatic dissemination (Figure 5D) were markedly reduced by the two HDAC inhibitors.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo treatment experiments shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Addition of panobinostat or romidepsin to cisplatin agonistically repressed PAX8 expression and elicited enhanced cleavage of PARP.
source: Remarkably, addition of panobinostat or romidepsin to cisplatin agonistically repressed PAX8 expression and elicited enhanced cleavage of poly-(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP), a marker of cells undergoing apoptosis, accompanied by profoundly downregulated pro-mitotic cyclin D1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data from combination treatment experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Combinatorial chemotherapy and HDAC inhibitors induced concurrent apoptotic and pyroptotic cell death in ovarian cancer.
source: Therefore, combinatorial chemotherapy and HDAC inhibitors induced concurrent apoptotic and pyroptotic cell death in ovarian cancer.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of cleaved PARP (apoptosis marker) and cleaved GSDME (pyroptosis marker) along with LDH release shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cell viability was synergistically inhibited by polytherapies combining cisplatin and HDAC inhibitors.
source: As a result, cell viability was synergistically inhibited by polytherapies, as demonstrated by dose matrix experiments (Figure 6B) and crystal violet staining (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by synergy score calculations and crystal violet staining shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: Both PAX8 expression and cell proliferation in chemo-resistant SKOV3 cells remained susceptible to panobinostat or romidepsin exposure.
source: We further generated a chemo-resistant SKOV3 clone and found that both PAX8 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) and cell proliferation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) remained susceptible to panobinostat or romidepsin exposure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in chemo-resistant cells shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: The cisplatin + panobinostat combination imparted a more significant suppression of tumor progression compared to single agents in PDX models.
source: Following ~4 weeks of treatment, the cisplatin +panobinostat combination imparted a more significant suppression of tumor progression compared to the single agents, with cancer regression achieved in EOC-002 (Figure 6D) and stable disease observed in EOC-004 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PDX treatment experiments shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: Reduced PAX8 expression in the presence of panobinostat was associated with deficient cell proliferation and survival in PDX models.
source: Immunohistochemical staining revealed reduced PAX8 expression in the presence of panobinostat, which was associated with deficient cell proliferation and survival (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data from PDX tumors shown in Figure 6F.

claim: PAX8 was focally amplified in a subset of TCGA ovarian cancer subjects.
source: PAX8 represented one of the first described ovarian lineage-specific oncogenes (Cheung et al., 2011), and indeed, was focally amplified in a subset of TCGA subjects (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TCGA copy number data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Many established oncogenes in distinct malignancies were detected by the modified COPA analysis including ERBB2 in breast cancer, MET in stomach tumor and BCL2 in leukemia/lymphoma.
source: As expected, many established oncogenes in distinct malignancies were detected including ERBB2 in breast cancer, MET in stomach tumor and BCL2 in leukemia/lymphoma.
evidence: This is based on the COPA analysis results described in the Results section.

claim: The analytic framework was exceptionally robust in spotting putative lineage-survival oncogenes including ASCL1, CDX2, IRF4, MITF, NKX2-1, PAX8 and SOX2.
source: In addition, we found that our analytic framework was exceptionally robust in spotting putative lineage-survival oncogenes. For example, ASCL1, CDX2, IRF4, MITF, NKX2-1, PAX8 and SOX2 were pinpointed as outliers in cell lines of their corresponding cancer tissue origins (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the COPA results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PAX8 was significantly associated with the majority of regulon components at the mRNA level in both EOC cell lines and TCGA primary neoplastic tissues.
source: In line with this notion, correlation estimation provided evidence that PAX8 was significantly associated with the majority of regulon components at the mRNA level in both EOC cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A) and TCGA primary neoplastic tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A-B.

claim: Neither PAX8 nor PAX8-responsive regulon predicted high-grade serous ovarian cancer patient prognosis using the median expression cutoff.
source: Neither PAX8 nor PAX8-responsive regulon predicted high-grade serous ovarian cancer patient prognosis using the median expression cutoff (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: FGF18 was specifically involved in regulating ovarian cancer cell migration without affecting tumor outgrowth.
source: Notably, PAX8, SOX17 and CLDN16 each appeared to sustain cell proliferation, albeit to varied extents, whereas PAX8, FGF18 and CDH6 evidently contributed to cell migration in these two models. Of particular importance, FGF18 was specifically involved in regulating ovarian cancer cell migration without affecting tumor outgrowth, which was verifiable across different models (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenogenotypic screen results shown in Figure 2F-G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: FGFR inhibitor BGJ398 abrogated FGF18-induced cell migration.
source: Moreover, FGFR inhibitor BGJ398 abrogated FGF18-induced cell migration (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transwell migration assays with FGFR inhibitor shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Immunofluorescent staining demonstrated abnormally enhanced focal adhesions in PAX8-depleted cancer cells.
source: Accordingly, immunofluorescent staining of paxillin and F-actin demonstrated abnormally enhanced focal adhesions in PAX8-depleted cancer cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Panobinostat potently diminished PAX8 signal within 24 hr in multiple ovarian cancer cell lines.
source: As an example, panobinostat potently diminished PAX8 signal within 24 hr in KURAMOCHI (Figure 3D), HEY, SKOV3 and OVTOKO cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Either panobinostat or romidepsin treatment efficiently eradicated PAX8 protein in a larger panel of ovarian cancer cell lines.
source: Extending our findings out of the screen, we evaluated the effects of panobinostat (pan-HDAC inhibitors) and romidepsin (class I HDAC inhibitors) in a larger panel of ovarian cancer cell lines. Either of the treatments efficiently eradicated PAX8 protein (Figure 3G) as well as PAX8-positive tumor cells (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot and cell viability data shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: Cell migration was sensitive to panobinostat or romidepsin exposure.
source: Besides verified growth inhibition by crystal violet staining (Figure 3I), cell migration was likewise sensitive to panobinostat or romidepsin exposure (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transwell migration assays shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Both HDAC inhibition and PAX8 depletion caused a global change of gene expression.
source: Both HDAC inhibition and PAX8 depletion caused a global change of gene expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), including the above-mentioned PAX8 regulon (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq heatmaps shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The most differentially expressed genes upon HDAC inhibition or PAX8 depletion were associated with generally overlapping pathways.
source: Although HDAC inhibitors exhibited comparably larger effects than PAX8 sgRNAs (Figure 4E), GSEA pinpointed that the most differentially expressed genes were associated with generally overlapping pathways across various conditions (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by gene ontology and pathway analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Lung adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma cell lines responded well to panobinostat or romidepsin regimens.
source: As anticipated, these cell lines responded well to panobinostat or romidepsin regimens (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by crystal violet staining of lung cancer cells treated with HDAC inhibitors shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Proteolytically cleaved gasdermin E (GSDME) was observed upon combination treatment with cisplatin and HDAC inhibitors.
source: Interestingly, we also observed proteolytically cleaved gasdermin E (GSDME), a newly recognized executor of cell pyroptosis (Lu et al., 2018; Rogers et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017), and consistently, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release was detected, indicating plasma membrane rupture and leakage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot showing cleaved GSDME and LDH release assay shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PAX8 was restrictedly expressed in two PDXs of epithelial ovarian cancer out of 221 models from seven different types of solid cancers.
source: To validate our observations, we assembled a patient-derived xenograft (PDX) cohort containing 221 models from seven different types of solid cancers, and RNAseq indicated that PAX8 was restrictedly expressed in two PDXs of epithelial ovarian cancer (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis of PDX models shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The PAX8 regulon as a signature approximately resembled the differential expression of PAX8 alone in subgroup comparison.
source: The PAX8 regulon as a signature approximately resembled the differential expression of PAX8 alone in subgroup comparison, that is upregulation in differentiated tumors and downregulation in immunoreactive tumors (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: PAX8 expression normally attenuates upon completion of ontogenesis but remains detectable in some confined areas throughout adulthood.
source: Upon completion of ontogenesis, PAX8 expression normally attenuates, but remains detectable in some confined areas throughout adulthood, for example fallopian secretory epithelial cells (Perets et al., 2013), possibly to fine-tune tissue homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Perets et al., 2013.

claim: Epithelial ovarian cancer is de facto Müllerian, rather than coelomic, in nature.
source: Recent evidence presented by Project Achilles supports that PAX8 is a prototype lineage-survival oncogene in epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC), the most lethal form of gynecologic malignancies which is de facto Müllerian, rather than coelomic, in nature based on epidemiological, histopathological, morphological, embryological, molecular, and experimental observations (Dubeau, 2008; Dubeau and Drapkin, 2013; Karnezis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies (Dubeau, 2008; Dubeau and Drapkin, 2013; Karnezis et al., 2017).

claim: Super-enhancers activate crucial cell identity genes and are sensitive to perturbation.
source: This conjecture is in line with the seminal work demonstrating that super-enhancers activate crucial cell identity genes and are sensitive to perturbation (Whyte et al., 2013), and also suggests that other lineage-survival oncogenes may likewise be susceptible to epigenetic interventions, a notion supported by our preliminary tests in lung cancer.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Whyte et al., 2013 and preliminary data in lung cancer models.

claim: Many lineage-survival oncogenes are likely vulnerable to epigenetic therapies.
source: This conjecture is in line with the seminal work demonstrating that super-enhancers activate crucial cell identity genes and are sensitive to perturbation (Whyte et al., 2013), and also suggests that other lineage-survival oncogenes may likewise be susceptible to epigenetic interventions, a notion supported by our preliminary tests in lung cancer.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PAX8, NKX2-1, and SOX2 (all lineage-survival oncogenes) are sensitive to HDAC inhibition.

claim: The Müllerian tract gives rise to fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix and the upper third of the vagina.
source: Mouse genetics studies reveal that PAX8 is restrictedly expressed in developing brain, thyroid, kidney, and Müllerian tract, from which the fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix and the upper third of the vagina originate.
evidence: This is based on established embryological knowledge.

claim: AR is a lineage-survival oncogene in prostate adenocarcinoma.
source: Notable examples of so-called lineage-survival oncogenes include AR (androgen receptor) in prostate adenocarcinoma (Visakorpi et al., 1995), CCND1 (cyclin D1) in breast cancer (Sicinski et al., 1995), MITF (melanogenesis associated transcription factor) in melanoma (Garraway et al., 2005), NKX2-1 (NK2 homeobox 1) in lung adenocarcinoma (Weir et al., 2007), SOX2 (SRY-box 2) in squamous cell carcinomas (Bass et al., 2009), ASCL1 (achaete-scute family bHLH transcription factor 1) in pulmonary neuroendocrine tumors (Augustyn et al., 2014), OLIG2 (oligodendrocyte transcription factor 2) in malignant glioma (Ligon et al., 2007), CDX2 (caudal type homeobox 2) in colorectal cancer (Salari et al., 2012), FLT3 (fms related tyrosine kinase 3) in acute myeloid leukemia (Stirewalt and Radich, 2003), IRF4 (interferon regulatory factor 4) in multiple myeloma (Shaffer et al., 2008), and lately identified PAX8 (paired box 8) in ovarian carcinoma (Cheung et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Visakorpi et al., 1995.

claim: CCND1 is a lineage-survival oncogene in breast cancer.
source: Notable examples of so-called lineage-survival oncogenes include AR (androgen receptor) in prostate adenocarcinoma (Visakorpi et al., 1995), CCND1 (cyclin D1) in breast cancer (Sicinski et al., 1995), MITF (melanogenesis associated transcription factor) in melanoma (Garraway et al., 2005), NKX2-1 (NK2 homeobox 1) in lung adenocarcinoma (Weir et al., 2007), SOX2 (SRY-box 2) in squamous cell carcinomas (Bass et al., 2009), ASCL1 (achaete-scute family bHLH transcription factor 1) in pulmonary neuroendocrine tumors (Augustyn et al., 2014), OLIG2 (oligodendrocyte transcription factor 2) in malignant glioma (Ligon et al., 2007), CDX2 (caudal type homeobox 2) in colorectal cancer (Salari et al., 2012), FLT3 (fms related tyrosine kinase 3) in acute myeloid leukemia (Stirewalt and Radich, 2003), IRF4 (interferon regulatory factor 4) in multiple myeloma (Shaffer et al., 2008), and lately identified PAX8 (paired box 8) in ovarian carcinoma (Cheung et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sicinski et al., 1995.

claim: MITF is a lineage-survival oncogene in melanoma.
source: Notable examples of so-called lineage-survival oncogenes include AR (androgen receptor) in prostate adenocarcinoma (Visakorpi et al., 1995), CCND1 (cyclin D1) in breast cancer (Sicinski et al., 1995), MITF (melanogenesis associated transcription factor) in melanoma (Garraway et al., 2005), NKX2-1 (NK2 homeobox 1) in lung adenocarcinoma (Weir et al., 2007), SOX2 (SRY-box 2) in squamous cell carcinomas (Bass et al., 2009), ASCL1 (achaete-scute family bHLH transcription factor 1) in pulmonary neuroendocrine tumors (Augustyn et al., 2014), OLIG2 (oligodendrocyte transcription factor 2) in malignant glioma (Ligon et al., 2007), CDX2 (caudal type homeobox 2) in colorectal cancer (Salari et al., 2012), FLT3 (fms related tyrosine kinase 3) in acute myeloid leukemia (Stirewalt and Radich, 2003), IRF4 (interferon regulatory factor 4) in multiple myeloma (Shaffer et al., 2008), and lately identified PAX8 (paired box 8) in ovarian carcinoma (Cheung et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Garraway et al., 2005.

claim: NKX2-1 is a lineage-survival oncogene in lung adenocarcinoma.
source: Notable examples of so-called lineage-survival oncogenes include AR (androgen receptor) in prostate adenocarcinoma (Visakorpi et al., 1995), CCND1 (cyclin D1) in breast cancer (Sicinski et al., 1995), MITF (melanogenesis associated transcription factor) in melanoma (Garraway et al., 2005), NKX2-1 (NK2 homeobox 1) in lung adenocarcinoma (Weir et al., 2007), SOX2 (SRY-box 2) in squamous cell carcinomas (Bass et al., 2009), ASCL1 (achaete-scute family bHLH transcription factor 1) in pulmonary neuroendocrine tumors (Augustyn et al., 2014), OLIG2 (oligodendrocyte transcription factor 2) in malignant glioma (Ligon et al., 2007), CDX2 (caudal type homeobox 2) in colorectal cancer (Salari et al., 2012), FLT3 (fms related tyrosine kinase 3) in acute myeloid leukemia (Stirewalt and Radich, 2003), IRF4 (interferon regulatory factor 4) in multiple myeloma (Shaffer et al., 2008), and lately identified PAX8 (paired box 8) in ovarian carcinoma (Cheung et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Weir et al., 2007.

claim: SOX2 is a lineage-survival oncogene in squamous cell carcinomas.
source: Notable examples of so-called lineage-survival oncogenes include AR (androgen receptor) in prostate adenocarcinoma (Visakorpi et al., 1995), CCND1 (cyclin D1) in breast cancer (Sicinski et al., 1995), MITF (melanogenesis associated transcription factor) in melanoma (Garraway et al., 2005), NKX2-1 (NK2 homeobox 1) in lung adenocarcinoma (Weir et al., 2007), SOX2 (SRY-box 2) in squamous cell carcinomas (Bass et al., 2009), ASCL1 (achaete-scute family bHLH transcription factor 1) in pulmonary neuroendocrine tumors (Augustyn et al., 2014), OLIG2 (oligodendrocyte transcription factor 2) in malignant glioma (Ligon et al., 2007), CDX2 (caudal type homeobox 2) in colorectal cancer (Salari et al., 2012), FLT3 (fms related tyrosine kinase 3) in acute myeloid leukemia (Stirewalt and Radich, 2003), IRF4 (interferon regulatory factor 4) in multiple myeloma (Shaffer et al., 2008), and lately identified PAX8 (paired box 8) in ovarian carcinoma (Cheung et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bass et al., 2009.

claim: ASCL1 is a lineage-survival oncogene in pulmonary neuroendocrine tumors.
source: Notable examples of so-called lineage-survival oncogenes include AR (androgen receptor) in prostate adenocarcinoma (Visakorpi et al., 1995), CCND1 (cyclin D1) in breast cancer (Sicinski et al., 1995), MITF (melanogenesis associated transcription factor) in melanoma (Garraway et al., 2005), NKX2-1 (NK2 homeobox 1) in lung adenocarcinoma (Weir et al., 2007), SOX2 (SRY-box 2) in squamous cell carcinomas (Bass et al., 2009), ASCL1 (achaete-scute family bHLH transcription factor 1) in pulmonary neuroendocrine tumors (Augustyn et al., 2014), OLIG2 (oligodendrocyte transcription factor 2) in malignant glioma (Ligon et al., 2007), CDX2 (caudal type homeobox 2) in colorectal cancer (Salari et al., 2012), FLT3 (fms related tyrosine kinase 3) in acute myeloid leukemia (Stirewalt and Radich, 2003), IRF4 (interferon regulatory factor 4) in multiple myeloma (Shaffer et al., 2008), and lately identified PAX8 (paired box 8) in ovarian carcinoma (Cheung et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Augustyn et al., 2014.

claim: OLIG2 is a lineage-survival oncogene in malignant glioma.

claim: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release indicates plasma membrane rupture and leakage.
source: Interestingly, we also observed proteolytically cleaved gasdermin E (GSDME), a newly recognized executor of cell pyroptosis (Lu et al., 2018; Rogers et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017), and consistently, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release was detected, indicating plasma membrane rupture and leakage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about LDH as a marker of membrane integrity.

claim: Cleaved PARP is a marker of cells undergoing apoptosis.
source: Remarkably, addition of panobinostat or romidepsin to cisplatin agonistically repressed PAX8 expression and elicited enhanced cleavage of poly-(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP), a marker of cells undergoing apoptosis, accompanied by profoundly downregulated pro-mitotic cyclin D1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cleaved PARP as an apoptosis marker.
